title: Current-mode logic (CML) transmit line driver with source-series termination
topology: A differential pair steered by a tail current source drives a pair of pull-up resistors (or a resistor-terminated current-mode output), with the pull-up resistor value chosen to match the transmission line's characteristic impedance (typically 50 ohm single-ended / 100 ohm differential) so the driver doubles as its own source (series) termination. Data is applied differentially to the pair's gates; the tail current switches fully between the two output legs each bit period, producing a constant-common-mode, voltage-mode output swing set by (tail current) x (termination resistance) rather than by supply rail swing, which keeps output impedance constant and well-matched across the whole bit period (unlike a simple push-pull CMOS driver whose output impedance varies through the transition).
spec_class: PHY-class transmit driver -- differential line driver for high-speed serial/wireline I/O (serdes, LVDS-class, chip-to-chip links) where constant output impedance and controlled slew/swing matter more than rail-to-rail voltage swing

pdk_portability.notes: The CML differential-pair-plus-resistive-termination topology is fully portable to any PDK with matched NMOS devices and precision (or trimmable) resistors; sky130 offers both (matched core devices, and precision poly or diffusion resistor options). What is sky130-specific is the achievable termination-resistor absolute-value accuracy (process variation on sky130's resistor options) and the tail current source's output impedance/matching, both of which set the actual line-impedance-match error and common-mode rejection achieved and must be characterized against sky130's process corners; a programmable/trimmed termination resistor (a small parallel resistor bank) is the standard PDK-independent mitigation for absolute resistor-value variation.

sizing_approach: Set the termination resistor value to the target line impedance (e.g. 50 ohm) directly, then size the tail current to hit the target differential output swing (swing = tail current x termination resistance) at the supply headroom available, trading a larger tail current (more swing, more power, more headroom needed) against a smaller one; size the differential-pair devices for sufficient transconductance to fully steer the tail current within the available input voltage swing at the target data rate, and size them wide enough that their own parasitic drain capacitance does not dominate the output pole at the target bit rate; where pre-emphasis/de-emphasis is required to compensate channel loss, add a second, smaller tail-current branch driven by a delayed/inverted copy of the data and sum its current into the same termination resistors, sizing that branch's current as a fraction (typically 10-30%) of the main-cursor current.
layout_idioms: differential pair and termination resistors laid out symmetrically on a common axis with matched, minimized routing length to both output pads to preserve differential balance and minimize skew between the two legs

termination resistors placed physically close to the output pads (not just electrically close) to minimize the parasitic trace inductance/capacitance between the intended termination point and the actual line launch point

tail current source transistor(s) laid out with adequate length and, where matching to a bias-generator current mirror, common-centroid placement to minimize output-current mismatch between the differential legs

wide, low-inductance supply and ground routing directly to the driver core, since CML drivers are current-steering (not voltage-switching) and are comparatively insensitive to supply noise but still sensitive to ground bounce coupling into the termination reference

source.citation: M. Mizuno, M. Yamashina, K. Furuta, H. Igura, H. Abiko, K. Okabe, A. Ono, and H. Yamada, "A GHz MOS adaptive pipeline technique using MOS current-mode logic," IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits, vol. 31, no. 6, pp. 784-791, June 1996.
source.license_or_openness: Peer-reviewed IEEE journal paper cited here for its MOS current-mode logic (MCML) differential-pair-plus-load topology and sizing tradeoffs only (no figures or text reproduced), per the KB's open-sources sourcing rule. This is a foundational reference establishing MOS current-mode logic as a practical CMOS circuit family; the resistively-terminated differential-pair driver used here for line driving is the same current-steering core circuit generalized to a transmit-driver application.

notes: Framed here specifically as a line driver (resistors sized to the channel impedance for source-series termination) rather than MCML's original use as an internal high-speed logic family, since PHY transmit drivers are the most common place this circuit reappears; the sizing methodology (tail-current-to-termination-resistance swing relationship) carries over directly. See rx-front-end-termination-buffer for the receive-side counterpart that this driver's matched line impedance is designed to terminate into.
